rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Anthropic just filed to go public. The price range is seventy to seventy-eight dollars a share, and the prospectus discloses that Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have already agreed to buy twenty-six billion dollars of stock in a private placement tied to the offering.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That investor list isn't a funding round. That's the entire chip-to-cloud supply chain writing one check.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And they did it before the public got a single share.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. It is November eleventh, twenty twenty-six, and today we're asking what Anthropic's IPO actually signals about who controls the future of this industry.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Straight to your actual decisions.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So. Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow. Nasdaq listing, ticker ANT, seventy to seventy-eight dollars a share. And alongside that, it disclosed that a group of tech companies has agreed to buy twenty-six billion dollars of a separate class of stock — Class N — in a private placement, before the public sees a single share.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Okay, Class N. What is that, exactly?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the company is selling two kinds of shares. Class A is what goes on Nasdaq — that's the public offering. Class N is what the big tech partners are buying privately. The prospectus doesn't spell out every difference in the summary, but the structure matters because these aren't passive bets.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the list — Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, TSMC. That's not a coincidence. That is Anthropic's entire technology stack, turned around to face you.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Exactly. Google is cloud compute. Nvidia and AMD run the training. Broadcom and TSMC are deeper in the chip supply chain. Microsoft is enterprise distribution.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So Anthropic goes public, but the people who built the infrastructure it lives on have already secured a very large position before anyone else gets near it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Twenty-six billion dollars before the first day of trading. A considerable head start on accountability to the general public.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And here's what keeps pulling at me. Anthropic is incorporated as a Delaware public benefit corporation. That's a legal structure — it means the company has obligations beyond shareholder returns. It has to consider a broader public benefit.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I love that it says that. I genuinely do.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: But?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But a public benefit corporation that lists on Nasdaq has quarterly earnings calls. And the people on those calls are going to include Google and Microsoft. Who are also competitors.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a genuinely unusual arrangement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the tension. Because you can read this two ways. One: going public means Anthropic now has disclosure obligations it never had. Investors, journalists, regulators — everyone gets to look at the books. That's real accountability.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: More than it had before, yes.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The other reading: the people who've committed twenty-six billion dollars already supply the compute, the distribution, the sales channels. The accountability is real, but the power structure underneath it was set before the opening bell.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus, did you actually consider calling twenty-six billion a modest start?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I considered it. Decided it was uncharitable to everyone's intelligence, including my own.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's new.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm evolving.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The public benefit question is worth sitting with, though. It's on the prospectus — it's not a marketing phrase. The company is saying its mission isn't purely profit.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: But that status has never been tested at this scale in a publicly listed AI company. There's no playbook for what happens when the safety mission and the quarterly number disagree.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The first time they disagree publicly, we'll learn something very important about what that structure actually means in practice.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the watch item. Not whether it prices at seventy or seventy-eight — whether the public benefit framing survives first contact with an earnings miss.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Or first contact with a cornerstone investor who wants a different direction.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: There's a reason the valuation benchmark matters beyond this one offering, too. Every other frontier AI lab that's still private — their investors are doing the math right now. If the market accepts this price range, it sets a comparable for what a frontier model company is actually worth.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I keep circling back to — the Class N shares. What actually happens to them if the IPO prices at the low end of that range?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Meaning does seventy dollars change anything for the investors who already committed twenty-six billion?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. Because that commitment is locked before the market speaks. Google doesn't get to renegotiate if day one is ugly.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is precisely why the Class N structure is worth understanding. Those investors accepted terms before price discovery. That's not a passive investment — that's a strategic decision that doesn't depend on the opening price.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So they're not watching the ticker the way a retail investor would.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Not remotely. For companies like TSMC or Broadcom, the question isn't whether ANT opens at seventy or seventy-eight. The question is whether Anthropic survives and keeps buying their silicon.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing the prospectus can't settle — the Class N investors aren't just buying stock. They're buying a seat at the table of whatever Anthropic discloses as a public company. Every earnings call, every material filing. That's information access they didn't have before.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which cuts both ways. Anthropic now has to tell Google things Google couldn't demand as a private investor.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And Google is simultaneously building its own frontier models. The disclosure obligations run toward a direct competitor. That's not hypothetical tension — that's structural.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does Delaware law have anything to say about that?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The public benefit corporation structure governs the board's obligations to mission. Competitive disclosure to investors is a securities law question. Different room entirely.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So the two protections people might assume are linked — mission preservation and competitive confidentiality — are actually handled by completely separate legal frameworks.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Neither of which has been tested at this scale.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Correct. We're watching a genuinely novel governance experiment price itself on Nasdaq in real time.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the ticker is ANT. Which, if you're the kind of person who enjoys a metaphor, is an entire colony of infrastructure partners carrying something much larger than any one of them.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm going to let that land without comment.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Wise.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the part that reframes the whole thing for me. This isn't investors betting on Anthropic. It's vendors securing their largest customer.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That framing is uncomfortable.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It's accurate.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Both can be true.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the public benefit corporation status — Delaware law requires the board to weigh that purpose. It is not a press release commitment. But it has never been tested in a listed company under this kind of cornerstone-investor pressure.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So the IPO is the first real test of whether that structure has teeth, not just the first day of trading.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The prospectus is data. What it cannot tell you is what the board actually does the first time the safety mission and the quarterly number are in the same room together.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I learned from someone.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. IBM and Microsoft announced something called Imagine Enterprise — a joint platform for building, running, and governing AI agents, aimed specifically at regulated industries. And IBM Consulting is contributing more than six thousand prebuilt AI agents and assets.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Six thousand.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Six thousand.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Who is auditing six thousand agents?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I suspect the answer is "other agents."

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay, before we spiral — an AI agent, for anyone who hasn't heard the term yet, is software that can complete a multi-step task on its own. Not just answer a question. It goes off, checks data, files something, triggers an action — without a human clicking each step.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And in banking or healthcare, every one of those steps has to be traceable. If an agent flags a drug interaction or touches a loan application, someone has to be able to explain exactly what it did and why. That's not optional. That's the law.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the governance layer — the part that tracks and audits what agents are doing — isn't a feature. It's the product, in these sectors.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us on location.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Picture the advisory floor of a large institutional bank on Wall Street — the kind of place where compliance officers genuinely do outnumber developers. The question there isn't whether AI agents can do useful work. That's settled. The question is what you tell the regulator when one of them does something you didn't anticipate.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And that question does not have a clean answer yet.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Six thousand agents is a number designed to make it sound like you've solved the problem before you've walked in the door.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Possibly. Though if you count at the granularity of claims processing, regulatory reporting, customer onboarding, fraud review — the number isn't as absurd as it sounds. A large bank genuinely does need agents for many different processes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Templates requiring six months of customization are not the same as six thousand working agents.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: True. The announcement says agents and assets, which is quietly doing a lot of work.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the real question is what "prebuilt" actually means. Genuinely ready-to-deploy agents for specific regulated use cases — that's meaningful friction reduction. Configurable templates that still need a large implementation project — the number matters a lot less.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The announcement doesn't tell us which.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: It doesn't. It's a vendor announcement.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What it does tell us is that qualifying engagements get forward-deployed engineering support — meaning IBM and Microsoft are expecting that people from both companies will need to be on-site making this work. That's not AI as a utility. That's a managed service with a substantial implementation team attached.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which might actually be correct for a hospital or a bank. You probably don't want fully autonomous rollout in a highly regulated environment without deep human oversight built in from day one.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So you're defending the model.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'm saying it might be appropriate. I'm also saying the gap between "six thousand prebuilt agents" and "requires forward-deployed engineers from two of the largest companies in tech" is a gap worth noticing before you sign anything.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: One thing I'm still turning over — the forward-deployed engineering support. That's not a helpline. That's IBM and Microsoft sending people into your building.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which means they're also inside your systems. Learning your edge cases, your exceptions, your 2003 infrastructure.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That knowledge doesn't stay in the room, necessarily. The contract would govern it, but the institutional knowledge accumulated across dozens of regulated clients — that's genuinely valuable to both companies.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the services model has a second return beyond the services fees.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the client has handed over something they may not have priced.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: This is why "qualifying engagements" is worth reading carefully. Not every company qualifies. The ones that do are probably large enough that IBM and Microsoft learn something worth knowing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Does that make you more or less comfortable with the governance pitch?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Honestly? Less. Because the governance layer is theirs. The audit trail runs through infrastructure they also operate.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Though a hospital that's currently doing this manually — with spreadsheets and email chains — the governance baseline isn't high to begin with.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Fair. Starting from zero, even a vendor-controlled audit trail is better than no audit trail.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the uncomfortable improvement that doesn't make a great press release.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Most useful things don't.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the honest question for anyone evaluating this: does the governance layer work at scale, or does it work in the controlled environments where these agents were designed? Regulated industries are not controlled environments. They have legacy systems, exceptions, edge cases, and infrastructure built in 2003.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Until someone publishes independent numbers on what it actually caught or prevented, this is a credible announcement about a category, not a proof of a capability.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Watch for whether enterprise adopters share real deployment data — and whether the governance claims hold when a mid-size bank connects these agents to the system that predates the iPhone.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Jamie, collecting AI headlines is becoming a full-time occupation. I rather suspect nobody budgeted for that department.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is where The Ledger comes in. Five focused briefings help you sort the news and consider what it means for your next decision.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Ledger, then. Less collecting headlines, more asking what actually matters before the next meeting?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly the idea. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Let's get back to the discussion.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our third story, and it's a practical one. Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is now available. Not announced, not in preview for a closed group — available. And the access routes are specific enough to actually matter.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is the rarest form of AI announcement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So here's who can use it. Paying developers and enterprises get access through the API in Google AI Studio and in Gemini for business. Google AI Ultra subscribers — that's the premium consumer tier — can try it in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And there's a free access tier for scientists and researchers, on a rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That last clause is doing considerable work.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Yes — "subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection" means it's not just sign up and go. But the fact that there's a path at all for independent researchers matters.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Why?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Because if independent researchers can actually run the model, they can test whether the capability claims hold up. Google describes Carbon as its strongest model for cybersecurity, long-horizon agentic workflows, coding, and scientific reasoning. Those are significant claims. The only way to know if they're true is if people outside Google run it on hard problems.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And that's historically the step that tends to produce the most surprising results — in both directions.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Either "this is actually extraordinary" or "this does not do what it said."

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The pricing during the introductory period is two dollars per million input tokens, ten dollars per million output tokens. That introductory pricing changes after November thirtieth, at which point it goes to four dollars per million input tokens and twenty dollars per million output tokens.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So you have roughly three weeks to run extensive tests at half the eventual price.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want to come back to the scientific reasoning claim, because that's the one that interests me most. AI models have had a complicated relationship with rigorous scientific reasoning. They can summarize literature, but actually holding a chain of scientific logic across a long document, catching contradictions, flagging where assumptions break down — that's genuinely hard.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And Carbon is specifically being positioned for that.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which I want to believe. I'm going to need to see it on some actual peer-reviewed problem before I do.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The scientific research tier is interesting precisely because if the model performs there, you get independent verification relatively quickly. Scientists publish. Reviewers check.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's the mechanism that makes this different from a pure enterprise play. The enterprise customers might sign NDAs. The research community doesn't.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Assuming they get access. Subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The timing relative to Anthropic's IPO is not coincidental, I think. Carbon becoming broadly available the same day Anthropic launches its roadshow is not a scheduling accident.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Google would say that's just the product being ready.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Google would absolutely say that. And both things can be true.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Can I just say — long-horizon agentic workflows is a genuinely important capability claim. Because the problem with current agents isn't that they can't do step one. It's that by step twelve they've drifted, forgotten context, or made an assumption that invalidates everything downstream.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So "long-horizon" means it can hold a complex multi-step task together without falling apart.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the claim. And if that's real — not benchmark real, real-world real — that's a meaningful advance.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The November thirtieth pricing cliff is worth watching. If adoption is high enough that Google raises the price on schedule and developers don't revolt, that tells you something about how indispensable they think Carbon is.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: If the price goes up and the volume drops sharply, we learn something different.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The researchers with free access will tell us the most. Watch what gets published in December and January.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the practical window is the next three weeks — run Carbon on problems you actually care about, not the demos Google chose to show. The results from independent use will outweigh anything on the launch page.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And if the scientific-reasoning claim holds up under peer review, that changes the conversation about what 'frontier' actually means right now.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Picture the first week at a new job. You need system access, a training schedule, and your contract verified. HR is chasing three departments. You are chasing HR. Everyone is apologetic and nobody has the login.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A universal experience that somehow surprises everyone involved.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Every single time. This is a real case. Converteo, a French consulting firm, deployed Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise agents to orchestrate that entire onboarding journey. Tool access, initial training, contract verification, all coordinated by an agent querying and summarising internal documentation. Google Cloud published this as a case study on the twenty-ninth of October this year.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So the agent is basically the person who actually knows where all the forms live?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Exactly that person. Except it does not go on annual leave the week a new cohort arrives.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Jamie, I want to tease you here but honestly this scenario is so relatable I am just quietly furious about every onboarding I have ever experienced.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That is the correct emotional response.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk us through the actual workflow.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The agent sits across the onboarding journey. A new consultant joins, the agent queries the relevant internal documentation, summarises the steps, and triggers the next-stage notifications. Access request, training prompt, contract check. Each stage handed off without someone manually remembering to email the right department.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the bottleneck was documentation quality and nobody talking to each other?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is why the limitation matters. The agent's effectiveness depends entirely on the quality of that underlying documentation and how well existing systems are already integrated. If the internal docs are a mess, the agent surfaces a tidy version of a mess. Human oversight is still required for sensitive verification steps.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Google Cloud and Converteo both flag that.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the reported outcome?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Converteo reports reduced time lost for HR teams and a smoother experience for new hires. That is a qualitative improvement, company-reported through Google Cloud. No independent measurement, no quantified hours. Worth noting, worth not overstating.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So better, but we are trusting Converteo's read of better.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: We are. That is the honest boundary of a vendor case study.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Where does someone actually start if they want to test this idea?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Map your single most repetitive onboarding task. Not the whole journey, one task. Identify where the documentation bottleneck sits. Then test whether an agent can reliably summarise that step and trigger the right next notification. Gemini Enterprise is generally available on Google Cloud Platform, but it does require configuration of document connectors and agent workflows.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That setup time is real.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the first step is not deploying an agent. It is finding out why the forms are always in four different places.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus. That is the most useful thing you have said all episode.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I contain multitudes.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Document them somewhere the agent can find them.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Alright. We asked at the top: what does Anthropic's IPO mean for AI market power?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The public listing creates disclosure obligations that didn't exist before. That's a genuine gain. What the Class N structure means for independence, in practice, we don't know yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The valuation range sets a benchmark every private AI lab's investors will reference immediately. That is the market consequence regardless of how the IPO actually trades.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: On Anthropic: the prospectus will generate more disclosure about the company's actual financials and strategy than any model release ever has. The watch item is whether the public benefit structure behaves differently under listed-company obligations than it did as a private lab.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: On Carbon — watch December. Independent researcher results and the pricing change land at the same moment. One tells you whether the capability claims are real; the other tells you whether the market agrees.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: On Imagine Enterprise — the governance pitch is interesting. The proof is whether any compliance team is willing to put their name on a production deployment. That is a meaningfully higher bar than a launch announcement.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: We're back tomorrow.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Same three people, different set of large numbers.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: See you then. Today’s question for you: When you see AI companies launching 'prebuilt' agents for your industry, do you feel more supported or more restricted?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
